sections.title: 1. Yield Measures — Current Yield and Dividend Yield
sections.overview: Yield expresses the cash income a security pays relative to its market price. Current yield (for bonds) and dividend yield (for stocks) are the simplest income-only measures and ignore capital gain/loss at maturity or sale. Both move inversely with price.
key_concepts: Current Yield (bonds): annual income from coupons divided by current market price; rises as bond price falls.
Dividend Yield (stocks): annualized cash dividend divided by current market price.
Nominal (Coupon) Yield: fixed at issuance; based on par value, not market price.
Inverse price/yield relationship: bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Yield hierarchy on a discount bond (priced below par): Nominal < Current Yield < YTM < YTC.
Yield hierarchy on a premium bond (priced above par): Nominal > Current Yield > YTM > YTC.
Par bond: Nominal = Current Yield = YTM = YTC.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.2 — Concepts of measurement: yield, YTM, YTC, total return, basis points.
formulas: Current Yield = Annual Coupon Interest / Current Market Price
Dividend Yield = Annual Dividend per Share / Current Market Price
Nominal (Coupon) Yield = Annual Coupon Interest / Par Value
1 Basis Point = 0.01% = 0.0001
mnemonics: Discount bond yield ladder "NC-Y-C" (low→high): Nominal, Current, YTM, YTC — premium bond reverses the order.

sections.title: 2. Yield to Maturity (YTM) and Yield to Call (YTC)
sections.overview: YTM and YTC are total-return-to-redemption measures that include both coupon income and the amortization of any premium or accretion of any discount over the remaining life of the bond. They are the yields most often quoted to investors and assume reinvestment of coupons at the same rate.
key_concepts: YTM: total annualized return if the bond is held to maturity; reflects coupon income plus gain (discount) or loss (premium) versus current price.
YTC: same calculation but to the earliest call date and call price; relevant for callable bonds trading at a premium.
Yield to Worst: the lower of YTM and YTC — what is quoted to the customer on a callable bond.
Premium callable bonds: YTC is the conservative (worst) yield because early call accelerates loss of premium.
Discount callable bonds: YTM is typically the worst case because early call accelerates the gain — investor would prefer the call.
Approximation of YTM uses straight-line amortization of premium/accretion of discount.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.2 — YTM and YTC are required measurement concepts.
formulas: Approx. YTM = [Annual Coupon + (Par − Price)/Years to Maturity] / [(Par + Price)/2]
Approx. YTC = [Annual Coupon + (Call Price − Price)/Years to Call] / [(Call Price + Price)/2]
Yield to Worst = min(YTM, YTC)
mnemonics: "Premium calls hurt — YTC is worst." "Discount calls help — YTM is worst."

sections.title: 3. Total Return
sections.overview: Total return is the comprehensive performance measure: it combines all income received (interest, dividends) with realized and unrealized capital appreciation or depreciation, expressed as a percentage of the original cost basis. Unlike yield, total return captures price change.
key_concepts: Components of return per SIE outline: interest, dividends, realized gains, unrealized gains, and return on capital.
Realized gain/loss: triggered by sale; taxable event.
Unrealized gain/loss: paper profit/loss on a position still held.
Return of capital (ROC): distribution that is not from earnings — reduces cost basis rather than being taxed as income currently.
Holding-period return vs. annualized return — SIE focuses on simple holding-period total return.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.2 — components of return and total return.
formulas: Total Return = (Income + Capital Gain) / Cost Basis
Holding Period Return = (Ending Value − Beginning Value + Income) / Beginning Value
Adjusted Cost Basis after ROC = Original Cost − Return of Capital received
mnemonics: "I-CG-CB": Income + Capital Gain, over Cost Basis.

sections.title: 4. Capital Gains and Losses — Realization, Holding Period, Wash Sale
sections.overview: A capital gain or loss arises when a security is sold for more or less than its adjusted cost basis. The federal tax rate depends on holding period: short-term (one year or less) is taxed as ordinary income; long-term (more than one year) qualifies for preferential rates. Wash-sale rules disallow losses on quick repurchases.
key_concepts: Short-Term Capital Gain (STCG): holding period of one year or less; taxed at ordinary income rates.
Long-Term Capital Gain (LTCG): holding period of MORE THAN one year; taxed at preferential 0% / 15% / 20% rates depending on taxable income bracket.
Holding period begins the day AFTER trade date of purchase and ends on trade date of sale.
Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT): additional 3.8% surtax on net investment income above MAGI thresholds.
Capital loss deduction: net capital losses offset capital gains; up to $3,000 of net loss deductible against ordinary income per year; excess carried forward indefinitely.
Netting order: short-term losses first offset short-term gains; long-term losses first offset long-term gains; then cross-netted.
Wash Sale Rule: loss disallowed if a "substantially identical" security is purchased 30 days BEFORE or 30 DAYS AFTER the loss sale (61-day window).
Disallowed wash-sale loss is ADDED to the cost basis of the replacement security and the original holding period tacks on.
Cost basis methods: FIFO (default), specific identification, or average cost (mutual funds).
Cost basis reporting: brokers must report basis for "covered" securities to the IRS.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.2 — cost basis requirements.
Errata 8.3 — LTCG requires holding period more than one year.
Errata 8.6 — Wash sale 30 days before/after; disallowed loss added to basis of replacement.
formulas: Capital Gain/Loss = Net Sale Proceeds − Adjusted Cost Basis
Adjusted Basis (wash sale replacement) = Purchase Price of Replacement + Disallowed Loss
Max Net Capital Loss Deductible vs. Ordinary Income = $3,000/yr (excess carried forward)
Wash Sale Window = 30 days before sale + sale date + 30 days after = 61 days
mnemonics: "More than a year for the lower-rate cheer" — LTCG = >1 year.
"30 BEFORE, 30 AFTER, 61 in all" — wash sale window.
"FIFO unless you say SO (Specific identification Otherwise)."

sections.title: 5. Taxation of Ordinary Income, Investment Income, and Dividends
sections.overview: Different categories of investment income are taxed under different schedules. Interest is generally ordinary income; qualified dividends receive LTCG rates; municipal bond interest is federally tax-exempt. The qualified-dividend holding-period test is a common SIE testable item.
key_concepts: Ordinary Income: wages, non-qualified dividends, short-term capital gains, taxable interest — taxed at marginal rates.
Corporate Bond Interest: fully taxable at federal, state, and local levels.
U.S. Treasury Interest: taxable at federal level; EXEMPT from state and local tax.
Municipal Bond Interest: EXEMPT from federal tax; may also be exempt from state/local tax if issued in the holder's state ("triple tax-free").
Private Activity Bond Interest: federally tax-exempt but a preference item for the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT).
Qualified Dividends: taxed at LTCG rates (0/15/20%); must be paid by a U.S. or qualified foreign corporation AND holder must satisfy holding-period test.
Qualified Dividend Holding Period: stock must be held more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days BEFORE the ex-dividend date.
Non-Qualified Dividends: REIT ordinary dividends, money-market fund dividends (interest), dividends on stock not meeting holding test — taxed as ordinary income.
Return of Capital distributions: not taxed currently; reduce basis; when basis reaches zero, further distributions are capital gains.
Tax-Equivalent Yield: lets investor compare muni yield to a taxable bond yield.
Accreted discount on OID municipal bonds is treated as tax-exempt interest (not capital gain).
Accreted discount on taxable OID bonds is taxable interest each year, even though no cash received.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.2 — investment returns and types of dividends.
Errata 8.5 — Qualified dividend holding test: >60 days within the 121-day window around ex-date.
formulas: Tax-Equivalent Yield = Municipal Yield / (1 − Investor's Marginal Federal Tax Rate)
After-Tax Yield (taxable bond) = Taxable Yield × (1 − Marginal Tax Rate)
Qualified Dividend Holding Test: >60 days held within 121-day window centered on ex-date (60 before / 60 after)
mnemonics: "PAB = AMT" — private activity bonds hit AMT.

sections.title: 6. Long-Term vs. Short-Term — Rate Application and Strategy
sections.overview: The single most important tax distinction at the SIE level is whether a position has been held long enough to qualify for long-term capital gain treatment. This drives both rate determination and customer tax-planning advice.
key_concepts: Short-Term: holding period of 1 year or less → ordinary income rates (currently up to 37%).
Long-Term: holding period of MORE THAN 1 year → 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income.
High earners also pay 3.8% NIIT on investment income above MAGI thresholds.
Holding period clock: starts day AFTER trade date of purchase; ends on trade date of sale.
Inherited securities receive automatic LONG-TERM treatment regardless of decedent's holding period; basis is generally stepped up to fair market value at date of death.
Gifted securities: donor's cost basis and holding period carry over to donee (for gain); for loss, basis is the lesser of donor's basis or FMV at date of gift.
Wash-sale and constructive-sale rules can extend or alter the holding period.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.2 — components of return.
Errata 8.3 — short-term = ordinary rates; long-term = >1 year.
formulas: Holding Period: Day After Purchase Trade Date → Sale Trade Date
If Holding Period > 365 days → Long-Term; else Short-Term
Inherited Stock Basis = FMV at date of death (stepped up); Holding Period = automatically long-term

sections.title: 7. Cost Basis Adjustments from Corporate Actions
sections.overview: Stock splits, stock dividends, return of capital, and wash sales all change a holder's per-share cost basis without necessarily creating an immediate taxable event. Understanding the mechanics is required by the SIE outline.
key_concepts: Forward Stock Split (e.g., 2-for-1): share count multiplied, per-share price and per-share basis divided proportionally; aggregate basis unchanged.
Reverse Stock Split (e.g., 1-for-10): share count reduced, per-share price and per-share basis multiplied; aggregate basis unchanged.
Stock Dividend: additional shares issued; aggregate basis spread across larger share count → lower per-share basis; not currently taxable.
Cash Dividend: taxable in year received; does NOT change basis.
Return of Capital: reduces cost basis dollar-for-dollar; taxable only after basis reaches zero (then capital gain).
Wash Sale: disallowed loss is added to basis of the replacement shares; original holding period tacks on.
Mergers / Tender Offers: cash received generally triggers capital gain; stock-for-stock exchanges often tax-deferred with carryover basis.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.4 — corporate actions and impact on cost basis.
formulas: New Per-Share Basis after Split = Old Aggregate Basis / New Total Shares
New Per-Share Basis after Stock Dividend = Old Aggregate Basis / (Old Shares + Dividend Shares)
Adjusted Basis after ROC = Original Basis − Return of Capital Received
Replacement Basis after Wash Sale = Purchase Price + Disallowed Loss
mnemonics: "Splits change SHARES and PRICE — never AGGREGATE basis."

sections.title: 8. Comparative Yield Analysis — Taxable vs. Tax-Exempt
sections.overview: Because municipal interest is federally tax-exempt and Treasury interest is state-exempt, investors must compare yields on an after-tax basis. Tax-equivalent yield is the standard tool for choosing between a muni and a taxable bond.
key_concepts: Higher marginal tax bracket → munis become MORE attractive relative to taxable bonds.
Lower bracket → taxable bonds (corporates/Treasuries) often beat munis on an after-tax basis.
Triple-tax-free munis: investor in own state of residence escapes federal, state, and local tax.
After-tax yield is the practical comparison metric for taxable bonds.
NIIT (3.8%) does not apply to municipal bond interest — adds to munis' relative advantage for high earners.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.2 — yield concepts and basis-point measurement.
formulas: Tax-Equivalent Yield = Tax-Exempt Yield / (1 − Marginal Federal Tax Rate)
After-Tax Yield = Taxable Yield × (1 − Marginal Tax Rate)
Break-Even: Tax-Exempt Yield = Taxable Yield × (1 − Tax Rate)
mnemonics: "DIVIDE for TEY; MULTIPLY for ATY." (Divide muni yield by 1−t; multiply taxable yield by 1−t.)

sections.title: 9. Dividend Mechanics and Tax Timing
sections.overview: Dividend payment dates determine who is entitled to receive a dividend and therefore when the tax liability attaches. The ex-dividend date is the pivot for both ownership and the qualified-dividend holding-period test.
key_concepts: Declaration Date: board announces the dividend.
Record Date: holders of record on this date receive the dividend.

Ex-Dividend Date: first day stock trades WITHOUT the dividend; under T+1 regular-way settlement, ex-date is the SAME business day as the record date (the buyer that day will not be on the record list).
Payable Date: dividend is paid out.
On ex-date, the stock price opens lower by approximately the dividend amount.
Cash dividends → taxable in year received (qualified or non-qualified).
Stock dividends → not currently taxable; spread basis across new share count.
Qualified-dividend status requires >60 days held in the 121-day window centered on ex-date.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §3.1.2 — dividend payment dates.
Errata: T+1 equity settlement (effective 5/28/2024) aligns ex-date with record date.
formulas: Ex-Date (regular-way, T+1) = Record Date (same business day)
Approx. Price Drop on Ex-Date ≈ Dividend per Share
Qualified Dividend Window = 121 days = 60 days before ex-date + ex-date + 60 days after
mnemonics: "DREP": Declaration → Record/Ex (same day under T+1) → Payable.
"Hold 61, save on one" — meet the 60-in-121 test to convert ordinary to LTCG rates.
